title: A generic method
summary: A method can have its own type parameter, so it works on a list of anything.

steps.title: A method with its own blank

say.never: Sometimes only one method needs a type blank, not the whole class. Put the type parameter just before the return type: `public static <T> T middle(List<T> items)`. Read it as "for any type T, take a list of T and give back one T". The `<T>` comes first so Java knows what `T` means in the rest of the line.
say.bit: `<T>` before the return type gives one method its own type parameter.

say.never: When you call a generic method, you don't write the type. Java looks at what you passed in and works out `T` itself. Pass a `List<String>` and you get a `String` back; pass a `List<Integer>` and you get an `Integer`. One method, every kind of list.
say.bit: Java works out T from the arguments: a `List<String>` in, a `String` out.

steps.title: In your lesson: A method with its own blank

say.never: `lastOrDefault` gives back the last item in a list, or a `fallback` you pass in when the list is empty. Both the list and the fallback use the same `T`, so Java makes sure they match: a list of autos and a default auto name, or a list of scores and a default score. The starter uses `Object`, which loses the type, so change it to `<T>`.
say.bit: `<T> T lastOrDefault(List<T> items, T fallback)`: the last item, or `fallback` when the list is empty.
